# Overview

Before combining survey items, I checked whether they measure one underlying idea and whether they are internally consistent. This report reviews **employee proficiency (Q3–Q6)** and **operational effectiveness (Q31–Q34)** using the results saved in the original report.

# Process and Key Findings

## 1. Check whether the items belong together

I reviewed the correlations, KMO and Bartlett’s test. The employee items showed stronger shared relationships, with **KMO = .78**. The operations items had **KMO = .50**, suggesting weak support for factor analysis. Bartlett’s test was significant for both sets, but significance alone does not establish a useful scale.

## 2. Examine the factor structure

The employee items supported one factor. Their loadings ranged from **.73 to .93**, and the factor explained approximately **63% of the variance**. Some fit statistics were less reassuring, so I would interpret the structure alongside the loadings and item wording rather than describe the fit as uniformly good.

For operations, the one-factor model was dominated by Q32. The remaining loadings were only **.23–.39**, while Q32 loaded near **1.00** with very low uniqueness. That boundary estimate calls for caution, even though the overall fit indices looked acceptable.

The saved parallel-analysis output suggested **two factors for operations**, contrary to the original explanation. However, an unrestricted two-factor EFA with only four items is not adequately identified, so I would not use that model to justify separate subscales. Parallel analysis also uses simulation; setting a seed makes future runs reproducible.

## 3. Check reliability and choose the measure

| Measure | KMO | Cronbach’s alpha | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| Employee proficiency: Q3–Q6 | .78 | **.87** | Combine into an employee index. |
| Operational effectiveness: Q31–Q34 | .50 | **.47** | Analyze the four items separately. |

Dropping an employee item lowered alpha. Dropping an operations item did not bring reliability close to .70. The wording supports the same decision: courtesy, helpfulness, professionalism and availability describe staff proficiency, while privacy, speed, service fit and application simplicity are different operational judgments.

# Implications for the Next Analysis

I will use the mean of Q3–Q6 for **R3** and the residence comparison in **R4a**. For **R6 and R4c**, I will keep Q31–Q34 separate. This four-item operations result (α = .47) differs from the earlier five-item Q30–Q34 analysis (α ≈ .54); they are different item sets.

Any one-sample t-test needs a stated comparison value. Residence comparisons involve independent groups, and testing several operations items requires attention to multiple comparisons.

# R Code

Code is grouped below; lengthy output and plots are hidden. The summaries above describe the supplied report’s saved results. Seeded parallel-analysis reruns may differ from its original unseeded run.

## Setup and checks

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(psych)
library(GPArotation)
library(knitr)
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")

if (!file.exists("Case 31 Data_efcu_4.sav")) {
  stop("Place Case 31 Data_efcu_4.sav beside this QMD before rendering.")
}
efcu <- read_sav("Case 31 Data_efcu_4.sav")
d    <- zap_labels(efcu)

r3_items <- c("q3", "q4", "q5", "q6")
r6_items <- c("q31", "q32", "q33", "q34")

r3 <- as.data.frame(d[, r3_items])
r6 <- as.data.frame(d[, r6_items])

item_labels <- c(
  q3  = "Q3: Employees are courteous",
  q4  = "Q4: Employees are helpful",
  q5  = "Q5: Employees are professional",
  q6  = "Q6: Employees are available",
  q31 = "Q31: Personnel keep info confidential",
  q32 = "Q32: Prompt in processing loans",
  q33 = "Q33: Services meet members' needs",
  q34 = "Q34: Loan applications simple"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: helpers
# Screening summary: KMO + Bartlett + eigenvalues
screen_scale <- function(x) {
  k  <- KMO(x)
  b  <- cortest.bartlett(cor(x), n = nrow(x))
  ev <- eigen(cor(x))$values
  list(kmo = k, bartlett = b, eigen = ev)
}

# Loadings table from a one-factor ML solution
loading_table <- function(f, x) {
  tibble(
    Item        = item_labels[colnames(x)],
    Loading     = f$loadings[, 1],
    Communality = f$communality,
    Uniqueness  = f$uniquenesses
  )
}

# Alpha item table
alpha_table <- function(a, x) {
  tibble(
    Item             = item_labels[colnames(x)],
    Mean             = a$item.stats$mean,
    SD               = a$item.stats$sd,
    `r.drop`         = a$item.stats$r.drop,
    `Alpha if dropped` = a$alpha.drop$raw_alpha
  )
}
```

## Employee proficiency

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r3-cor
#| tbl-cap: "R3 inter-item correlations"
cor(r3) |> round(2) |> kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: r3-screen
r3_screen <- screen_scale(r3)
r3_screen$kmo
r3_screen$bartlett
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-r3-scree
#| fig-cap: "R3 parallel analysis and scree plot"
#| fig-height: 4.5
set.seed(3103)
r3_pa <- fa.parallel(r3, fm = "ml", fa = "fa", main = "R3 (Q3–Q6): parallel analysis")
```

```{r}
#| label: r3-efa
r3_fa <- fa(r3, nfactors = 1, fm = "ml", rotate = "none")
print(r3_fa, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r3-load
#| tbl-cap: "R3 one-factor ML solution"
loading_table(r3_fa, r3) |> kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: r3-alpha
r3_alpha <- alpha(r3)
r3_alpha$total |> kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r3-alpha
#| tbl-cap: "R3 item-total statistics"
alpha_table(r3_alpha, r3) |> kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: r3-composite-check
employee_index <- rowMeans(r3, na.rm = TRUE)
employee_index[is.nan(employee_index)] <- NA_real_
if ("Att_employee" %in% names(d)) {
  all.equal(employee_index, as.numeric(d$Att_employee))
}
```

# Reflection

The most useful part for me was seeing why a group of questions should not automatically become one score. Both sets use agreement scales, but only the employee items showed enough consistency to support combining them.

The operations results also reminded me to check the output against my explanation. A significant test or a good fit statistic is not enough on its own. I need to consider the loadings, reliability and what the questions actually ask before deciding how to use them.
